lead: The receiver must decide which known pulse arrived while noise blurs it. At the sampling instant t = T, one filter gives the largest signal-to-noise ratio: the matched filter, whose impulse response is the pulse reversed in time and delayed by T. A multiplier followed by an integrator produces the same sample and is called the correlation receiver. Digital modems, radar and optical receivers use this idea to squeeze the best error rate from a given pulse energy.
prereq: You need: 5.4 for the inner product and Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and Unit 1 for white noise and power spectral density.

sections.h3: The filter that maximises the sample

blocks.text: A known pulse s(t) lasts T seconds and has energy E = ∫₀ᵀ s²(t) dt. It arrives as r(t) = s(t) + n(t), where n(t) is white Gaussian noise with two-sided power spectral density N₀/2 W/Hz. Pass r(t) through a linear filter h(t), and sample the output at t = T. The signal part at that instant is y<sub>s</sub>(T) = ∫₀ᵀ h(τ)s(T − τ)dτ. The output noise variance is σ² = (N₀/2)∫₀ᵀ h²(τ)dτ. We want the largest possible ratio y<sub>s</sub>²(T)/σ².

blocks.where: h(τ) is the filter impulse response; s(t) is the known pulse; T is the pulse duration in seconds; E = ∫₀ᵀ s²(t)dt is the pulse energy in joules; N₀ is the one-sided noise density in W/Hz, so N₀/2 is the two-sided density; SNR(T) is the signal-to-noise ratio at the sampling instant.

blocks.text: Cauchy-Schwarz gives the upper bound. Equality needs h(τ) proportional to s(T − τ). Choose gain 1: h(t) = s(T − t). Its transfer function is H(f) = S*(f)e^(−j2πfT). This is the matched filter, also called the optimum filter for white noise. At t = T the signal output is E, the noise variance is N₀E/2, and the peak SNR is 2E/N₀ = E/(N₀/2).

The output for the signal alone is the autocorrelation R<sub>s</sub>(t − T) = ∫ s(u)s(u + t − T)du, shifted so its peak sits at t = T. The filter folds the pulse about T, so every part of the pulse adds in phase at the sampling instant. Its output at other times is not optimum; an early or late clock loses SNR.

sections.h3: Correlation receiver gives the same sample

blocks.text: Multiply r(t) by a stored copy of s(t) and integrate from 0 to T. The result at the dump instant is z(T) = ∫₀ᵀ r(t)s(t)dt = E + ∫₀ᵀ n(t)s(t)dt. The noise term has zero mean and variance (N₀/2)∫₀ᵀs²(t)dt = N₀E/2. The signal sample is E, exactly as with the matched filter. The multiplier, integrator and dump form the correlation receiver, also called the correlation detector; the dump resets the integrator for the next pulse.
z(T) = ∫₀ᵀ r(t)s(t)dt = E + n<sub>s</sub>,   Var(n<sub>s</sub>) = N₀E/2
blocks.where: z(T) is the correlator output at time T; r(t) is the received signal; s(t) is the stored pulse; E is the pulse energy in joules; n<sub>s</sub> is the noise component at the sample; N₀ is the one-sided noise density in W/Hz.

blocks.text: Equivalence is one change of variable. The matched filter output at T is y(T) = ∫ h(τ)r(T − τ)dτ = ∫₀ᵀ s(u)r(u)du = z(T). The two receivers make the same decision. The matched filter is convenient in hardware because it is a fixed filter; the correlator is convenient in analysis because it is an inner product, the same picture as 5.4.

items: The maximum SNR depends only on E and N₀, not on the pulse shape. For fixed energy in white noise, shape changes bandwidth and implementation, not the bound.
The factor 2 belongs there. With two-sided density N₀/2, the bound is E/(N₀/2) = 2E/N₀. Reporting E/N₀ is 3 dB low.
The bound is reached only at t = T. Sampling early or late, or using the filter output between samples, is suboptimal.
The matched filter maximises SNR; it does not remove intersymbol interference. Zero-ISI pulse shaping and equalisation are separate jobs (see 5.1 and 5.3).
For coloured noise, whiten the noise first; the plain matched filter is optimum only for white noise.

blocks.text: The next step, comparing this sample with a threshold to choose a symbol, is in 5.6.

figure.caption: The received signal splits into a matched filter branch and a multiply-and-integrate branch; both give the same sample at t = T, which then goes to the threshold and the decision.

spec.title: Two ways to build the same receiver
spec.aria: The received signal splits into a matched filter branch and a multiply-and-integrate branch; both give the same sample at t = T, which then goes to the threshold and the decision.

examples.question: A rectangular pulse of amplitude A = 1 V and duration T = 1 ms is received in white noise with one-sided power spectral density N₀ = 2 × 10⁻⁶ W/Hz. (a) Find the pulse energy. (b) Find the maximum signal-to-noise ratio at the matched-filter sampling instant, as a ratio and in dB. (c) Find the equivalent amplitude ratio √SNR.
steps: For a rectangular pulse, s(t) = A for 0 ≤ t ≤ T, so E = A²T = (1 V)² × (1 × 10⁻³ s) = 1 × 10⁻³ J = 1 mJ. The unit check is V²·s = W·s = J.
The two-sided noise density is N₀/2 = (2 × 10⁻⁶)/2 = 1 × 10⁻⁶ W/Hz.
examples.answer: The pulse energy is 1 mJ, the maximum output SNR is 1000 or 30 dB, and the equivalent amplitude ratio is about 31.6; any other filter shape gives a smaller value at t = T.
examples.check:
import math
A = 1.0
T = 1e-3
N0 = 2e-6
E = A*A*T
snr = 2*E/N0
snr_db = 10*math.log10(snr)
amp = math.sqrt(snr)
print(E*1000)
print(snr)
print(snr_db)
print(round(amp, 1))

traps: The commonest slip is to mix N₀ with N₀/2 and report E/N₀. The correct maximum is 2E/N₀, so E/N₀ is 3 dB low.
The matched filter maximises SNR only at t = T. Sampling early or late, or using its output between samples, is not optimal.
It does not cancel intersymbol interference. Zero-ISI pulse shaping and equalisation are separate jobs (see 5.1 and 5.3).
For an asymmetric pulse, h(t) = s(t) is wrong; it must be s(T − t), the time-reversed and delayed copy.
For coloured noise the plain matched filter is not optimum; whiten the noise first.

quiz.q: State the impulse response and transfer function of the matched filter for a pulse s(t) of duration T.
quiz.a: h(t) = s(T − t); H(f) = S*(f)e^(−j2πfT), where S(f) is the Fourier transform of s(t).

quiz.q: Why does time reversal align the pulse with the filter?
quiz.a: It makes the filter weights equal to the pulse samples in reverse order, so all signal contributions add in phase at t = T; this is the equality case of Cauchy-Schwarz.

quiz.q: A pulse has energy E = 2 mJ and the noise one-sided density is N₀ = 4 × 10⁻⁶ W/Hz. Find the maximum SNR as a ratio and in dB.
A receiver uses h(t) = s(t) for an asymmetric pulse. Is it matched? What happens to the peak SNR?
quiz.a: No, unless s(t) is symmetric. It gives less than 2E/N₀ at t = T; only h(t) = s(T − t) reaches the bound.

quiz.q: What operations define the correlation receiver?
quiz.a: Multiply r(t) by s(t), integrate from 0 to T, and sample at T. This is integrate and dump.

quiz.q: Show in one line why the matched filter and correlator give the same sample at T.
quiz.a: With h(τ) = s(T − τ), y(T) = ∫₀ᵀ h(τ)r(T − τ)dτ = ∫₀ᵀ s(u)r(u)du = z(T).

quiz.q: Why does sampling at T/2 reduce performance even if the filter is matched?
quiz.a: The signal output has not reached its peak E, so less signal energy is collected while the noise variance is fixed; SNR at T/2 is below 2E/N₀.

beyond: Not for the exam. Matched filtering is the correlation step inside every GPS receiver, radar pulse compressor and spread-spectrum rake receiver. In digital communications the same operation appears as a filter matched to the transmit pulse, followed by sampling. In MIMO and fading channels it becomes space-time combining. Search for matched filter bound, rake receiver and pulse compression radar.
